PRIVATE HOSPITALS AMENDMENT BILL 
Serial 82 

 
Mr EDGINGTON (Health): Madam Speaker, I present a Bill titled Private Hospitals Amendment Bill 2026, 
Serial 82 and table the explanatory statement. 
 
I move that the Bill be now read a first time. 
 
Motion agreed to; Bill read a first time. 
 
The purpose of this Bill is to amend the Private Hospitals Act 1981 to recast the regulatory and administrative 
framework to ensure Territorians have access to the full scope of private healthcare closer to home. It will 
also deliver on our governments commitment to bring back choice for Territory mothers and families through 
reinstating private maternity services at Darwin Private Hospital. 
 
The Private Hospitals Act has been in place for 45 years and these amendments represent the first 
substantial changes since 2011. 
 
The Bill expands the objects of the Act beyond protecting the health and welfare of people receiving treatment 
in private hospitals to including the planning and provision of healthcare services. The amendments create 
a dual mechanism for placing conditions on a private hospital licence issued under the Act to determine how 
medical, surgical or treatment services are to be provided. 
 
The first mechanism is through an imposed condition. This creates the power for the Department of Health 
Chief Executive Officer to impose conditions on a private hospital licence without limiting the scope of what 
an imposed condition might cover. Imposed conditions might range from conditions relating to the provision 
of private obstetric maternity services or any other matter the Department of Health chief executive thinks fit. 
 
The second mechanism is through a prescribed condition. This enables the Administrator of the Northern 
Territory to prescribe a private hospital as a designated private hospital. Once prescribed, additional or 
different conditions set out in the regulations may be applied to the designated private hospitals licence. 
 
This government will utilise these provisions to ensure Territorians have access to private obstetric maternity 
services. This Bill provides certainty by making it clear that where there is an inconsistency between a 
condition imposed by the Chief Executive Officer and a prescribed condition, the prescribed condition 
prevails. 
 
Furthermore this amendment preserves the ability for a licensee to seek a variation of an imposed condition 
while make clear that prescribed conditions remain enforceable and may only be amended by the 
Administrator of the Northern Territory. 
 
Our government has been clear from the start that private maternity must be restored in the Territory to 
ensure health equity and the long-term sustainability of our health system. Our government will work with the 
new operator of the Darwin Private Hospital on a sustainable pathway for this to happen. The powers afforded 
to the Department of Health Chief Executive in this Bill modernise the Act to reflect interstate practices. 
 
With this reform, there will now be explicit mechanisms to allow comprehensive, balanced and coordinated 
health services. It allows the Department of Health Chief Executive Officer to assess how delivery of holistic 
services across the Territory will occur and to ensure Territorians can access private services like maternity 
services here in the Territory.

A number of amendments throughout the Bill replace references to the Chief Health Officer with the 
Department of Health Chief Executive Officer. While the Chief Health Officer's primary role is focused on 
public health, wellbeing, and disease prevention, responsibility for regulating commercial enterprises more 
appropriately sits with the Chief Executive Officer of the Department of Health. 
 
These amendments are consistent with the principles of the Health Service Act 2021. They support safe, 
high quality and locally responsive health services, place the interests of patients at the centre of decisionmaking and recognise the important contribution of private community sector providers in delivering 
integrated healthcare across the Territory. 
 
This reform recognises that private hospitals are an important part of the Territory broader health system. By 
broadening the objects of the Act, the Bill supports a more coordinated and strategic approach to healthcare 
planning, helping to ensure services are delivered in a way that is comprehensive, balanced and responsive 
to community needs. The amendments bring much needed certainty around the expectations placed on 
private hospitals operating in the Territory. 
 
These amendments will help restore the Territory lifestyle and rebuild the economy by delivering a stronger 
regulatory framework and improving confidence and transparency within both the private and public health 
sector. It will also support private clinicians to live and work in the Northern Territory and enable regionallybased families to receive health services closer to home, reducing the need to travel interstate. 
 
We want a sustainable private hospital sector that meets the needs of Territorians. Legislative changes and 
important first step. I am pleased to commend this Bill to honourable members and table a copy of the 
explanatory statement. 
 
Motion agreed to; Bill read a first time. 
 

SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDERS 
Condemnation of the Member for Gwojas Comments About the Death of Kumanjayi Little Baby 

 
Ms CAHILL (Children and Families): Madam Speaker, I move to suspend so much of standing and 
sessional orders that would otherwise prevent debate on the following motion without notice that the 
Assembly: 
 
1. condemns the Member for Gwoja for his public comments on Tuesday 20 October 2026 about the death 

of Kumanjayi Little Baby, which were broadcast on the ABC, published in the Guardian and the NT News 
and posted on the members own TikTok account 

 
2. notes those comments were made while criminal proceedings over her death are before the courts 

 
3. recognises the hurt those comments caused 

 
4. calls on the Member for Gwoja to withdraw his comments and apologise. 
 
Leave granted. 
 

MOTION 
Condemns the Member for Gwoja for Comments About the Death of Kumanjayi Little Baby 

 
Ms CAHILL (Child Protection): Madam Speaker, I move that the Assembly: 
 
 condemns the Member for Gwoja for his public comments on Tuesday 20 October 2026 about the death 

of Kumanjayi Little Baby, which was broadcast on the ABC, published in the Guardian and the NT News 
and posted on the members own TikTok account 

 
 notes those comments were made while criminal proceedings over her death are before the courts 
 
 recognises the hurt those comments cause 
 
 calls on the Member for Gwoja to withdraw his comments and apologise. 
 
In April a five-year-old girl went missing in Alice Springs. For five days hundreds of people from across the 
Territory and around the country poured into Alice Springs to help find her. Police, volunteers, family and

people who had never met her covered every inch of ground they could, desperate to bring that precious little 
girl home. Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal people in Alice Springs, the communities the Member for Gwoja 
represents and across the country had their hearts in their throats for those five days. Then our worst fears 
came true. 
 
The loss of Kumanjayi Little Baby is one of the most devastating things this Territory has ever lived through. 
It rocked the nation and we grieved together. 
 
I commissioned the Independent Review into the Conduct of the Department of Children and Families 
because her family and every Territorian deserved to know how the system meant to protect her had failed 
her. On Tuesday I tabled that report in this place, and the government has accepted all 45 recommendations. 
That day should have been about her. 
 
Instead, the Member for Gwoja went to the media. I will read his comments to the Assembly: This alleged 
violent perpetrator was released from prison with no house, no transport, no job, no supervision and no 
rehabilitation or integration plan. Shadow Child Protection Minister Chansey Paech said that is why we no 
longer have Kumanjayi Little Baby here; it is because the justice and Corrections systems under the CLP 
failed. Those words were broadcast on the ABC, printed in the Guardian and the NT News and the member 
posted them on his TikTok. This was not a slip of the tongue at a doorstop; he chose to say it and then he 
chose to share it. 
 
A man has been charged over the death of this little girl, and that matter is before the courts. Every member 
of this Assembly knows what that means. We choose our words carefully because what matters most now 
is that justice is done for her and seen to be done. 
 
The Member for Gwoja knows it better than most; he was the Attorney-General of the Northern Territory. Yet 
he stood in front of the cameras and told Territorians that the alleged perpetrator was released from prison 
with no house, no transport and no job and that is why we no longer have Kumanjayi Little Baby here. That 
is reckless indifference to the delivery of justice and it is not something this Assembly can let pass. 
 
He was just as reckless about the hurt he caused. Think about her family hearing those words. Think about 
the people of Alice Springs who searched for five days. On the day the report into how the system failed her 
was tabled, the Member for Gwoja chose to focus himself on the rights of offenders, not her, not what she 
went through and not her family. This is offender-focused commentary and it is condemnable. It is also 
nothing new from those opposite. 
 
For eight years Labor's answer to crime in this Territory started with the offender and worked backwards. 
This government starts with the victim. That is why we passed the Every Child Matters Bill and why the safety 
of a child now comes first in law. 
 
Labor has clearly learned nothing. The review the member was responding to was into the conduct of the 
Department of Children and Families, the department Labor ran for eight years. Its findings reach back across 
those years. 
 
In the same week the member admitted Labor could have done more. Within hours he was pointing the finger 
everywhere but at the system his own government left behind. There is no justification the Member for Gwoja 
can offer for these commentsnot grief, politics or frustration with the government. 
 
Kumanjayi Little Babys family deserve better and so does our community. 
 
This motion draws a line in the sand. Territorians expect their leaders to put victims first, respect the courts 
and think before they speak about the death of a child. If the Leader of the Opposition does not agree with 
her members comments, she has the opportunity to say so today by supporting this motion. 
 
The Member for Gwoja should withdraw his comments and apologies to Kumanjayi Little Babys family. 
 
I commend the motion to the Assembly.

Kumanjayi Little Baby and all those in the community who want to see their government calling out disgusting, 
indefensible, offending and cruel behaviour in our community. The community wants everyone in this 
Chamber standing up for victims and the community.

victims and belittled and made a front-on attack on the public servants who work day-in, day-out. It is time 
for the member to stop defending those offenders and making excuses for offending. It is time for him to 
stand up for victims and the community. 
 
Losing a child would be terrible. How would the mother and the family feel? What about the friends and those 
hundreds of people who went looking for this little baby? The community of Alice Springs jumped in behind 
to support them. The community of Alice Springs, under the last eight years of Labor, turned into chaos. The 
crime was through the roof and people were leaving. Alice Springs was in the media for all the wrong reasons.

through the floor. It is really lies at the Member for Gwojas feet because he was the minister for eight years. 
 
Linking the death Little Baby to a suggested political failure is absolutely disgusting. He needs to make sure 
that he focuses on the community and community safety. 
 
Here is a reminder of what happened under watch, when he was the Corrections minister and Deputy Chief 
Minister. He oversaw a dangerously crowded system where prisoners ended up in watch houses. There was 
no rehabilitation, no education, no training and no chance to break that cycle of reoffending. He stopped the 
rehabilitation and training programs. He clogged up the police watch houses and stopped the police from 
going out and keeping the community safe. That is an important point: he not only failed the Corrections 
system but also stopped the police from doing the very job that the community expects, which is to keep the 
community safe. It is shameful. 
 
He also oversaw a riot that caused $40m worth of damage to the Corrections system. That damage was 
done under his watch. There was not only the damage to public assets, but that riot was within the education 
system of Corrections, so it stopped the education and rehabilitation. 
 
The Member for Gwoja came out and said that is the justice systemjust thrown out with no training and no 
rehabilitation. We have spent two years in office. We have brought back the training and rehabilitation. In 
fact, one program we brought back is the Ready for Work program, which supports offenders when they 
leavefor the last 18 months or soto make sure they reintegrate back into society. 
 
This is what the Member for Gwoja could have done. He was the minister and the Deputy Chief Minister, but 
he failed to do that. He failed to put community safety above all else. He failed to listen to the voices of 
victims.

has now deleted, so he knows what he has done is wrong. He has gone away. His actions again speak

not have done that.

perpetrator was released from prison with no house, no transport, no job, no supervision and no rehabilitation 
reintegration plan. That is why we no longer have Kumanjayi Little Baby here.

want to just put the victims rights at the bottom. The victim needs to come first; the community needs to

brief. 
 
At its heart, this Bill relates to a straightforward economic problem: how do we make sure that major marine 
infrastructure can operate commercially, attract investment and recover efficient costs, while also ensuring 
that businesses that need to use the infrastructure can access it on a fair and reasonable basis? 
 
That balance is important because marine facilities are not ordinary markets. Major facilities like ship lifts, 
berths and associated marine infrastructure are expensive to build and have significant fixed costs. In many 
cases there will simply not be multiple competing facilities sitting side by side. That can create what 
economists describe as a natural monopoly or, at the very least, a significant infrastructure bottleneck. 
 
When access to one piece of infrastructure determines whether another business can compete in an 
upstream or downstream market, the way access is allocated and priced needs to be carefully considered. 
That is recognised expressly in this Bill. Its object is to promote the economically efficient operation and use 
of and investment in major marine facilities while promoting effective competition in upstream and 
downstream markets. 
 
There is a reasonable body of Australian research dealing with these issues. Taylor and McDonald, in their 
recent study of Australian container port reform, identify the natural monopoly characteristics that can exist 
at the port authority level and the potential for market power to flow through into rents and infrastructure 
access charges. Their broader point is that introducing private investment or commercial discipline does not 
by itself create a competitive market where the underlying infrastructure remains difficult or impossible to 
duplicate.

The purpose of economic regulation should not be to prevent an operator from making a commercial return
quite the opposite. If we want investment in marine infrastructure, the framework has to recognise the efficient 
cost of providing the service and the commercial risks involved. 
 
Equally, if a business has no realistic alternative to a piece of infrastructure, simply telling the parties to 
negotiate is not always enough. Research by John Black from the University of New South Wales and Violeta 
Roso looking at Port Botany after privatisation, makes a related point. Their analysis describes a model where 
private operators continue to play a major commercial role, but government retains important regulatory, 
planning and infrastructure responsibilities. They found that a robust and enforceable regulatory framework 
can co-exist with private investment and operation. That is broadly the balance this Bill is seeking to establish. 
 
The opposition supports the appointment of the Utilities Commission as the independent regulator. We also 
support the basic access architecture in the Bill. 
 
There is a presumption of access on a first-come first-served basis, subject to sensible exemptions for 
existing commercial contractual rights, queuing arrangements and flexible booking principles. These are 
defined processes for both standard and non-standard applications, including when modifications to a facility 
may be required. Importantly, operators are required to negotiate in good faith and access agreements must 
deal with matters including price, timing, capacity, maintenance responsibilities, performance criteria and 
dispute resolution. The protections against discriminatory conduct are also incredibly important. 
 
The Bill prevents an operator from hindering access and addresses circumstances where an operator, 
particularly one that is vertically integrated, may have an incentive to provide more favourable terms to itself 
or a related business. That goes directly to one of the central issues in infrastructure access regulation. It is 
not enough for access to exist on paper if the terms of that access can materially disadvantage a competitor. 
 
The pricing provisions are worth noting. The Bill does not just say that prices should be cheap; it adopts 
orthodox economic regulation principles. Prices should allow the operator to recover the efficient costs of 
providing access and receive a return consummate with the regulatory and commercial risks involved. At the 
same time, the framework provides for productivity incentives and seeks to prevent a vertically integrated 
operator using its terms and conditions to favour its own downstream operations. 
 
The Bill also gives the regulatory framework some flexibility. Depending on circumstances, regulation can 
range from monitoring prices and applying pricing principles through to maximum prices, revenue controls or 
other forms of economic regulation. That is sensible because not every facility will necessarily require the 
same degree of intervention. 
 
The ring-fencing provisions are another important safeguard. Requiring separate accounts for regulated 
services makes it easier for the regulator to understand the actual costs of providing those services, while 
protections around commercially sensitive information reduce the risk that information supplied by a customer 
could be used to disadvantage that customer elsewhere in the market. 
 
Finally, the statutory review mechanism is also an important part of this Bill. After the initial four-year period, 
and subsequently every five years, the regulator must examine whether access and price regulation remains 
necessary; whether the form of regulation remains appropriate; and whether the pricing principles themselves 
remain suitable. 
 
The real test of this legislation will ultimately be in its implementation, the regulations, the quality of the price 
determinations, the information available to the Utilities Commission and the capacity of the regulator to 
respond where problems arise. 
 
The framework established by this Bill recognises the right issues: investment; efficient pricing; open access; 
transparency; competitive neutrality; and protection against the exercise of infrastructure market power. For 
those reasons, the Territory Labor opposition supports the Bill.

whose activities contribute to the need for monitoring make an appropriate contribution to its cost while 
ensuring that the monitoring network will remain independent, government managed and publicly 
accountable. This framework will be prescribed in the regulations.

Protection Authority, as the regulator, has reliable data on which to make decisions. This Bill supports that.
